questiontext.text:
A student wants to prove each claim below by exhaustion, using the cases shown. For each one, choose finite and exhaustive if the cases would do the job, not exhaustive if some number the claim is about lies in none of the cases, or not finite if the list of cases never ends.

  1. A claim about {@dom1@}. Cases: {@cs1@}.

    [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

  2. A claim about {@dom2@}. Cases: {@cs2@}.

    [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

  3. A claim about {@dom3@}. Cases: {@cs3@}.

    [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

  4. A claim about {@dom4@}. Cases: {@cs4@}.

    [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt4]]

generalfeedback.text:
A set of cases works for a proof by exhaustion when it is finite, so the proof can be finished, and exhaustive, so every number the claim is about lies in at least one case.

  1. A claim about {@dom1@}, with cases {@cs1@}. {@labsent(cor1)@} {@expl1@}

  2. A claim about {@dom2@}, with cases {@cs2@}. {@labsent(cor2)@} {@expl2@}

  3. A claim about {@dom3@}, with cases {@cs3@}. {@labsent(cor3)@} {@expl3@}

  4. A claim about {@dom4@}, with cases {@cs4@}. {@labsent(cor4)@} {@expl4@}

questionnote.text: Rows {@map(first, qrows)@}; answers {@[cor1, cor2, cor3, cor4]@}

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the two conditions on the cases in Step 1 of a proof by exhaustion (the cases must be finite and exhaustive), pp. 13-14, in Section 5 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.
